Why connected devices need cybersecurity

IoT systems exchange information through networks and may also issue commands to physical equipment. This creates benefits, but it also means that a weakness in a connected device or its platform may expose information or permit unauthorised actions.

Cybersecurity involves protecting devices, data and systems against unauthorised access, modification, disruption and other digital risks. In IoT, cybersecurity can be important not only for information privacy but also for the safe functioning of physical equipment.

Common security risks

  • Unauthorised access: A person without permission gains access to a device or platform.
  • Weak authentication: The system does not adequately verify the identity of a person or device requesting access.
  • Exposed information: Personal, operational or location data becomes available to an unintended party.
  • Insecure software: An uncorrected weakness creates an opportunity for misuse.
  • Loss of availability: A device or service cannot communicate or operate when required.

The seriousness of a risk depends on the application. Exposure of a connected household sensor's data may affect privacy. Interference with a connected industrial controller could also affect physical equipment and operations.

Basic measures for protecting IoT systems

The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) identifies core capabilities for improving IoT-device cybersecurity. At a school-level understanding, the central ideas are straightforward:

  • Device identification: The system should be able to distinguish the device from others.
  • Authentication: A system should verify an identity before granting access where verification is required.
  • Authorisation: A verified user or system should have only the permissions appropriate to its role.
  • Data protection: Sensitive information should be protected against unauthorised access and alteration. Encryption can support this purpose.
  • Secure updates: Software changes should come through authorised and trustworthy processes.
  • Monitoring and recovery: Problems should be detectable, and systems should have appropriate procedures for responding to faults and restoring service.

Authentication and authorisation are not the same. Authentication asks who is requesting access; authorisation determines what that identity is permitted to do.

Privacy and responsible use

Connected devices may collect information about a person's location, health, household activities or electricity use. Even when collecting such data serves a legitimate purpose, the system should handle it according to applicable requirements and reasonable privacy safeguards.

Useful protections include limiting collection to necessary information, restricting access, retaining records only as needed and ensuring that authorised users understand the purpose of the monitoring. In healthcare, particular care is necessary because the information may be sensitive and decisions can affect patient wellbeing.

Distinguishing related technologies

Robotics, AI, automation and IoT often appear together in examples, but each term refers to a different function.

TechnologyDefining ideaWhat is not automatically required
RoboticsProgrammed physical action by a robotic mechanismInternet connectivity or human-like appearance
AutonomyCarrying out specified tasks without continuous human commandsUnlimited decision-making ability
IoTInterconnected things exchanging information for useful servicesMoving parts or physical actuation
Artificial intelligenceComputational methods for tasks such as pattern recognition and predictionA physical robot
Cloud computingNetwork-accessible computing and storage resourcesSensors or robotic movement

Applying the distinctions to real situations

A robotic vacuum cleaner operating locally can be a robot with limited autonomy even when disconnected from the Internet. A connected smart electricity meter can be an IoT device without being a robot. A connected warehouse robot can combine robotics with IoT because it both performs physical tasks and communicates useful operational information.

Likewise, a program that analyses stored photographs using AI is not automatically a robot. A connected temperature monitor is not automatically autonomous. A system should be classified by what it actually does rather than by whether it is marketed as smart or intelligent.

Prelims focus

  • Authentication verifies identity; authorisation determines permitted actions.
  • Secure software updates and data protection are important IoT cybersecurity capabilities.
  • IoT cybersecurity protects devices, information and connected services.
  • A locally operating autonomous robot need not be connected to the Internet.
  • A connected meter can be an IoT device without being a robot.
  • Trap: The terms robotics, autonomy, IoT, AI and cloud computing are related but not interchangeable.

[Sources: NIST, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline, NISTIR 8259A, May 2020, core technical capabilities, accessed 2026-11-05; NIST, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capabilities Catalog, technical capability categories, accessed 2026-11-05; ITU-T Recommendation Y.4218, May 2023, section 3.1, IoT device and infrastructure definitions, accessed 2026-11-05; International Federation of Robotics, Service Robots, explanation of autonomy under ISO 8373:2021, accessed 2026-11-05; NCERT, Informatics Practices, Class 11, Chapter 2, sections 2.2.4 and 2.4–2.5, accessed 2026-11-05.]
